notes.subject: plate
notes.text: White plates with a blue strip on the left holding the flag and GE, in the format AA-123-CD (two letters, three digits, two letters). Latin letters only.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Plates since 2014 have a small security hologram at the bottom right; the older three-letter format AAA-123 stays valid until 2030.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: A squarer two-line plate exists for imported North American or Japanese cars; motorcycles use two lines in the form AA/1234.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Older plates (1993 to 2014) are plain black on white in the format AAA-123, with GEO and later GE on the left; some show a flag.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Embassy vehicles have white characters on a red background.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Temporary plates have red letters and a red outline, starting with GA, GE, GG, GC or GP followed by four digits.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Cars in the breakaway northern regions use Russian-style plates in one and Soviet-style plates in the other; national plates are not used there.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: A unique script, written left to right; the modern alphabet has 33 letters and looks like no other writing system.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Two older scripts, capital-like and ornamental, survive only in church texts and icons; the everyday script is the modern one.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: The main language belongs to a small family unrelated to any other language family in the world.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Web domains end in .ge or in the local script (.გე); the phone code is +995.
